beats.narration: One drop of soap, and floating pepper races to the edge of the bowl. Nothing touched it. So what pulls the pepper?
beats.title: What pulls the pepper?
beats.source: Roché et al. · PRL 2014 · model illustration

beats.narration: Not the soap. Clean water further out pulls harder than the soapy spot, and drags the surface outward. In one lab study, that surface reached up to half a metre per second.
beats.title: Clean water pulls harder
beats.source: Roché et al. · PRL 2014 · model illustration

beats.narration: Yet with soap fed in steadily, the rush stops at a ring. Why there?
beats.title: Ring under steady feeding
beats.source: Roché et al. · PRL 2014 · model illustration

beats.narration: Here is the engine. At twenty five degrees, clean water pulls harder than our soap, SDS at an inferred twenty five millimolar in water: a gap of about thirty six millinewtons per metre, calculated. That gap, not the soap itself, does the pulling.
beats.title: Tension drives flow
beats.source: NIST · Liu · Roché · 25°C · SDS 25mM (inferred)

beats.narration: Every patch of that surface pulls on its neighbours. Over clean water the pull is strong; over the soapy spot it is weaker.
beats.title: Surface pull changes
beats.source: Roché et al. · PRL 2014 · model illustration

beats.narration: Over clean water the pull is strong; over the soapy spot it is weaker. The surface is dragged outward, and the water just below is dragged along. A flow driven by a difference in pull like this is called a Marangoni flow.
beats.title: Surface drags water
beats.source: Roché et al. · PRL 2014 · model illustration

beats.narration: How do you measure such a flow? Roché and colleagues pumped soap solution steadily through a fine needle onto centimetre-thick layers of ultrapure water, rated eighteen point two megohm centimetres. Olive oil droplets ten micrometres across were added to scatter light and trace the motion.
beats.title: Measuring the flow
beats.source: Roché et al. · PRL 2014 · model illustration

beats.narration: They tested eight surfactants, bought ninety nine per cent pure, with different tails and heads. Their micelle thresholds span two orders of magnitude. One of them is SDS. Another study measured its threshold at twenty five degrees, with no salt added: eight point two three, in millimolar units.
beats.title: Molecular differences
beats.source: Chenyakin & Chen · 25°C · SDS in water

beats.narration: Why does that threshold matter here? Below it, extra molecules crowd onto the surface. Above it, they clump into micelles in the water. Roché's model takes the threshold, the critical micelle concentration, as the soap concentration right at the needle.
beats.title: Crowding at the surface
beats.source: Roché et al. · PRL 2014 · model illustration

beats.narration: Now the balance. The gap in pull, spread over the size of the soapy patch, must be matched by friction inside a thin moving layer of water. In Roché's model, viscosity times surface speed over that layer's thickness roughly equals the gap over the patch radius.
beats.title: A balance of stresses
beats.source: Roché et al. · PRL 2014 · model illustration

beats.narration: Back to the bowl. Pepper grains float, so they ride on the surface. When the surface slides outward, the grains go with it. Roché's paper opens with this very trick: the grains, it says, are transported rapidly to the edge of the bowl.
beats.title: Pepper follows the surface
beats.source: Roché et al. · PRL 2014 · model illustration

beats.narration: Under steady pumping, Roché saw three zones: the source at the needle, a clear zone around it where tracers are swept away, and an outer zone with pairs of swirls.
beats.title: Three flow zones
beats.source: Roché et al. · PRL 2014 · model illustration

beats.narration: Outside the clear zone, the surface barely moves. The paper puts it plainly: further from the source, the tracers move only slightly. So the fast flow is confined. It fills the clear zone and no more.
beats.title: Beyond the clear zone
beats.source: Roché et al. · PRL 2014 · model illustration

beats.narration: Inside the clear zone the surface starts slowly, around one centimetre per second near the needle. It speeds up, reaching a peak near half a metre per second, then slows gradually as it crosses the rest of the zone.
beats.title: Speed builds then falls
beats.source: Roché et al. · PRL 2014 · model illustration

beats.narration: Then comes the surprise. At the edge of the clear zone, the gradual slowdown turns sudden. The tracers decelerate abruptly, and the fast surface flow ends right there. That edge is the ring from the start.
beats.title: A sudden slowdown
beats.source: Roché et al. · PRL 2014 · model illustration

beats.narration: Where does the water go? It cannot pile up at the edge. Below the clear zone, the paper traces a flow that follows the bottom of the container back towards the source. Surface out and bottom back make one loop.
beats.title: Water returns below
beats.source: Roché et al. · PRL 2014 · model illustration

beats.narration: Pump faster, and you might expect a faster flow. Not here. For one shorter tailed sulfate, the paper reports that the injection flow rate has little effect on the velocity field. What pumping does change is the size of the clear zone.
beats.title: Feeding changes the radius
beats.source: Roché et al. · PRL 2014 · model illustration

beats.narration: Tail length matters far more. Double the number of carbon atoms in the tail, and the radius of the clear zone changes over almost two orders of magnitude. Longer tails have lower micelle thresholds and make bigger zones.
beats.title: Longer tails, larger zones
beats.source: Roché et al. · PRL 2014 · model illustration

beats.narration: The head matters too. Keep a twelve carbon tail and swap only the head: the sulfate head of SDS gives a smaller clear zone than a trimethylammonium bromide head. Same tail, different head, different ring.
beats.title: Molecular heads
beats.source: Roché et al. · PRL 2014 · model illustration

beats.narration: Now the open question: why does the flow stop at a ring? Molecules leave the needle. Each one rides the surface outward, but it can also leave the surface and dissolve into the water below.
beats.title: Soap leaves the surface
beats.source: Roché et al. · PRL 2014 · model illustration

beats.narration: Roché's model rests on one assumption: the flow stops when the injected surfactants have all desorbed from the interface. Past that point the surface is clean again, the pull is even, and nothing drives the flow. The ring marks where soap runs out on the surface.
beats.title: Why the flow stops
beats.source: Roché et al. · PRL 2014 · model illustration

beats.narration: How fast should the surface go? Roché's speed law, with its constant set to one, uses the pull gap, viscosity, density and patch size. Take our gap of about thirty six millinewtons per metre, water's viscosity at twenty five degrees, and Roché's own patch estimate of fifteen millimetres: zero point four six metres per second, calculated.
beats.title: Estimating surface speed
beats.source: NIST · Liu · Roché · 25°C · SDS 25mM (inferred)

beats.narration: That lands close to the half a metre per second Roché measured. The same model gives the thickness of the moving layer: the square root of kinematic viscosity times patch size over speed. That is zero point one seven millimetres, calculated. A sheet that thin drags the surface across the dish.
beats.title: A thin moving layer
beats.source: NIST · Liu · Roché · 25°C · SDS 25mM (inferred)

beats.narration: The soap layer is thinner still. Soap molecules spread through water far more slowly than motion does. The paper's ratio, the Schmidt number, is roughly ten thousand. Its square root sets the gap, so the soap layer is a hundred times thinner, calculated.
beats.title: A thinner soap layer
beats.source: Roché et al. · PRL 2014 · model illustration

beats.narration: Now the ring size. Roché's second law says the zone radius grows with the pumping rate to the power three quarters, and shrinks as the micelle threshold rises. Double the pumping, and the ring grows one point six eight times, calculated. With a threshold of ten millimolar, the paper's estimate is fifteen millimetres.
beats.title: Predicting the ring radius
beats.source: Roché et al. · PRL 2014 · model illustration

beats.narration: Two more checks. Make the water layer more viscous and the zone grows, as the paper's supplement shows. And the speed law fails when the clear zone is as small as the millimetre long meniscus around the needle tip.
beats.title: Where the model fails
beats.source: Roché et al. · PRL 2014 · model illustration

beats.narration: So that is why the rush stops at a ring: in Roché's model, past it the soap has left the surface. And the ring is useful. The authors suggest estimating the micelle threshold from a single measurement of the zone's size at a known pumping rate, plus one independent surface tension measurement.
beats.title: Reading the threshold
beats.source: Roché et al. · PRL 2014 · model illustration

beats.narration: Time for the card on the bench. Three kinds of numbers appear on it: measured by Roché and colleagues, measured for SDS, and calculated from both.
beats.title: Three kinds of evidence
beats.source: Roché et al. · PRL 2014 · model illustration

beats.narration: Measured: surface speeds from about one centimetre per second near the needle to a peak near half a metre per second, and a zone radius that changes almost a hundredfold as tails double. The paper does not state a temperature, so these numbers carry none.
beats.title: Measured surface speeds
beats.source: Roché · PRL 2014 · temperature not stated

beats.narration: Calculated: a pull gap of about thirty six millinewtons per metre, a surface speed of zero point four six metres per second, a moving layer of zero point one seven millimetres, a soap layer a hundred times thinner, and a ring one point six eight times wider for double the pumping.
beats.title: Calculated quantities
beats.source: NIST · Liu · Roché · 25°C · SDS 25mM (inferred)

beats.narration: Our assumptions. Roché's constants are set to one, as in the paper. The patch size is Roché's estimate, not our measurement. The gap uses the SDS value at an inferred twenty five millimolar, while that estimate assumed a threshold of ten millimolar and a surface tension gap of its own.
beats.title: Model assumptions
beats.source: NIST · Liu · Roché · 25°C · SDS 25mM (inferred)

beats.narration: What we leave out. Pepper grains are not the paper's oil droplets. A kitchen bowl gets one drop, not a steady pump, so its ring is not fixed. And household dishwashing liquid is a mixture; our numbers are for SDS.
beats.title: Limits of the experiment
beats.source: Roché et al. · PRL 2014 · model illustration

beats.narration: Water's capillary length at twenty degrees came to two point seven three, in millimetres. SDS opens a gap in pull of about thirty six millinewtons per metre. That gap drives the surface at zero point four six metres per second, calculated.
beats.title: From capillarity to flow
beats.source: NIST · Liu · Roché · 25°C · SDS 25mM (inferred)

beats.narration: So the pepper is not pushed by the soap. Clean water pulls the surface away from the soapy spot, and under steady feeding the flow ends where the soap has left the surface. Try it with a bowl, some pepper and one drop of dish soap.
beats.title: Clean water pulls
beats.source: Roché et al. · PRL 2014 · model illustration
